transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The 2026 midterms are on track to be the most expensive on record.
According to the latest campaign finance filings,
Democratic candidates and Elon Musk dominated the last fundraising period.
Here's NPR's Stephen Fowler.
Musk added more than a quarter billion dollars in new contributions to Republican politics,
including more than $150 million to a super PAC aimed at the Texas Senate race.
That's more than Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Tallarico
have raised combined the entire midterm cycle.
Speaking of Tallarico, his record-setting third quarter,
60-plus million dollar haul leads the way for Democratic Senate nominees,
who vastly outraised their opponents in four out of every five cases.
Just look at the 13 races the Cook Political Report rates as competitive.
Republicans are being outraised by at least a five to one margin.
That, and how the parties are spending money,
suggests both parties are preparing for a potential blue wave.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
Russia says it is not ruling out a possible meeting with China and the U.S.
on the sidelines of an economic summit next month.
A spokesperson reacted to a Wall Street Journal report that
Russian leader Vladimir Putin suggested it.
NPR has not independently verified that story.
This, as more diplomatic fractures surface between the U.S. and Ukraine
over Kiev's ongoing attacks on Russia's oil refineries,
NPR's Charles Means reports President Trump accuses his counterpart,
Volodymyr Zelensky, of trying to drive up fuel prices in the U.S.,
even though many economists have tied the price surge to Trump's war with Iran.
It seems to be trying to protect Russian oil facilities.
Following a deal he cut with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel,
a move Trump hopes will bring down the price of gas for U.S. voters
ahead of midterm elections.
So in that sense, the news of Ukraine striking energy facilities
in St. Petersburg Sunday is unlikely to please Trump,
who's already called previous strikes, including one against Moscow,
last week a disgrace.
Charles Means reporting.
The company, Anthropic, says it is setting up a public benefit fund
for charitable donations.
The company says it's committing 5% of its shares to the fund.
NPR's John Ruich has details.
After raising money in May, Anthropic said it was valued at close to a trillion dollars,
and some analysts say the IPO could double that.
So the new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will be substantial,
and the company says more shares will go into the fund as Anthropic's valuation grows.
As for the kind of donations that the fund could make,
Anthropic says an example could be in the labor market,
which many experts expect AI to disrupt.
Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing the challenge.
The new fund, it says, could enable the company to take bolder action.
John Ruich, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Well, AI has become very good at tracking the paths of hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean.
Not as much in the Pacific.
Here's W.U.S.S. Jessica Massares.
Google DeepMind's AI model was spot on about Hurricane Isaias's path in the Gulf,
while missing the mark for Hurricane Simon in the Eastern Pacific.
Brian McNoldy, a hurricane researcher at the University of Miami, says,
AI doesn't use complicated math and science the way conventional prediction models do.
It makes us a little uncomfortable because we like to know why you're getting the right answer.
And I feel like we don't, or at least I don't.
AI creates forecasts based on patterns from thousands of past storms and atmospheric data.
Forecasters say Google DeepMind's projection for storm strength also needs some work.
That's Jessica Massares.
Researchers are learning more about how psychology influences the ability to bounce back from a sports injury.
Here's NPR's Will Stone.
A sizable share of people, about one in three, who undergo ACL surgery don't return to their previous level of sport.
Fear of being re-injured is often a big reason.
Shelby Bias directs the psychology of sports injury lab at UNC Chapel Hill.
In a new study, she and other researchers followed about 60 people recovering from ACL surgery
and ran a series of physical and psychological tests.
It wasn't necessarily those objective factors or quad strength and hop symmetry
that were predictive or associated with psychological readiness.
In her work at UNC, Bias is finding that certain approaches, like mindfulness and grounding techniques,
can be helpful for people who are cleared to play but still struggle with anxiety and fear after their injury.
It's NPR.
